title: Radioactive Decay Dating with Half-Life
learningObjectives: Interpret half-life as the time for one-half of a parent isotope to decay and apply it as a geologic clock.
Use the decay law N=N0*(1/2)^(t/T) to calculate the amount of parent isotope remaining after elapsed time t.
Compare remaining amounts for different half-lives and elapsed times to estimate geologic age.

explanations.text: A chemical element can exist as different isotopes with the same number of protons but different atomic weights. Radioactive decay is a spontaneous nuclear process where a parent isotope loses particles to form a daughter isotope of a new element.

evidence.quote: Atoms of the same element with differing atomic weights are called isotopes.
Radioactive decay is a spontaneous process in which an isotope (the parent) loses particles from its nucleus to form an isotope of a new element (the daughter).

explanations.text: The decay rate is described by half-life: the time required for one-half of the radioactive atoms in a sample to decay. After each half-life the remaining amount is halved.

evidence.quote: The rate of decay is conveniently expressed in terms of an isotope's half-life, or the time it takes for one-half

explanations.text: Most isotopes decay quickly within days or years, but a few decay slowly over billions of years. Those slow-decaying isotopes serve as geologic clocks for dating ancient rocks.

evidence.quote: Most radioactive isotopes have rapid rates of decay (that is, short half-lives) and lose their radioactivity within a few days or years.
Some isotopes, however, decay slowly, and several of these are used as geologic clocks.

predictions.prompt: A 100-gram Uranium-238 sample is buried. Uranium-238 has a half-life of 4.5 billion years. How much remains after 4.5 billion years?
Same 100-gram Uranium-238 sample after 9.0 billion years (two half-lives).
A 200-gram Potassium-40 sample (half-life 1.25 billion years) after 2.5 billion years.
